newsitem.title: UK: SmithKline launches ovarian cancer drug in UK.
newsitem.headline: SmithKline launches ovarian cancer drug in UK.

text.p: A new treatment for ovarian cancer, which kills thousands of women every year, was launched in Britain on Friday, the makers SmithKline Beecham Plc said.
The company said in a statement that Hycamtin, which won marketing approval in the U.S. in May 1996, had been approved in Britain for patients who failed to respond to chemotherapy.

Ovarian cancer is a poorly treated condition. Of the 5,000 women in Britain who contract the disease every year around 4,400 die. It is particularly tricky to diagnose because it is almost completely without symptoms in its early stages. Around three-quarters of all patients are not diagnosed until the tumour has spread beyond the ovaries.
"Ovarian cancer is frequently difficult to cure because it is often not detected until it has reached an advanced stage," said Martin Gore, consultant cancer physician at the Royal Marsden Hospital.

SmithKline Beecham said women who relapse within six months of their first course of drug or chemotherapy treatment are unlikely to respond to the same therapy a second time. Hycamtin "now becomes a logical second-line treatment for the condition, increasing the range of effective therapies available for the clinician," it said.

Another ovarian cancer treatment, Bristol Myers Squibb Co's Taxol, was approved last year for first-line treatment. SmithKline Beecham pointed to data presented at a recent scientific meeting, which it said showed a higher response rate from patients treated with Hycamtin and longer survival rates compared with Taxol. Hycamtin is the first of a new class of drugs, topoisomerase I inhibitors, which kill cancer cells by inhibiting a key enzyme.
The company said the main side-effect of Hycamtin was suppression of blood cells produced in bone marrow, although it said this was "predictable, reversible, manageable and non-cumulative."
